main.title: Golden Joystick Awards 2005
main.summary: The Golden Joystick Awards, with every category winner of the 2005 edition.

cards.heading: The players' awards
cards.text: The Golden Joystick Awards celebrate games through a public vote, bringing players into the choice of each year's winners. The awards began in Britain with the 1983 season and later reached an international audience through online voting. Their changing categories trace the growth of games: home computers and consoles, handhelds, online play, independent studios, performance and music. Alongside the public vote, special honours recognise individual contributions to the industry. Each edition preserves its own category names, so the results also show what players and the awards organisers considered worth celebrating at the time.

main.title: Mario Party 7
main.subtitle: A cruise with room for eight
main.summary: Mario Party 7 is Hudson Soft's final GameCube entry in the series, released in North America on 7 November 2005.

cards.heading: A cruise with room for eight
cards.text: Mario Party 7 is Hudson Soft's final GameCube entry in the series, released in North America on 7 November 2005. Toadsworth hosts a cruise through six themed boards, each offering a different way to compete for Stars. The game also expands some modes and minigames to eight people. Its party grows through pairs sharing resources and decisions, adding another layer of cooperation to a format normally driven by individual turns. A teammate becomes someone to consult before the next dice roll or item choice.

cards.heading: Each destination changes the value of a Star
cards.text: The boards attach different rules to earning Stars. Pagoda Peak changes their price as players reach the summit, Pyramid Park encourages stealing with Chain Chomps, and Windmillville ties Stars to ownership of windmills. These differences make the destination more than a new background for the same purchase. The player must first understand what resources or positions matter there. Coins earned in minigames can become the means of claiming an investment, buying an opportunity or taking a prize directly from another competitor.

cards.heading: Share the plan with a partner
cards.text: In team modes, partners move together and share coins, Stars and Orbs, alternating responsibility for choosing routes and items. The minigames can split the gathering into several configurations, including challenges built for eight participants. Microphone activities return alongside ordinary controller games. Hironobu Yahata and Shinya Outouge again composed the music. The cruise brings the GameCube run to a close by increasing both the size of the gathering and the variety of board rules, making agreement within a team as useful as winning against the others.

main.title: SOCOM U.S. Navy SEALs: Fireteam Bravo
main.subtitle: A tactical squad travels onto PSP
main.summary: SOCOM U.S. Navy SEALs: Fireteam Bravo is Zipper Interactive's portable tactical shooter, first released in North America on 8 November 2005. It brings the SOCOM approach to PSP through a third-person campaign and wireless multiplayer. The player enters missions with military equipment and the need to recognise threats before committing to an approach. Moving onto a handheld also required changes to the familiar console controls. The result places the series' interest in armed teamwork within a machine whose single analogue nub cannot reproduce the controller layout of the PlayStation 2 games directly.

cards.heading: A tactical squad travels onto PSP
cards.text: SOCOM U.S. Navy SEALs: Fireteam Bravo is Zipper Interactive's portable tactical shooter, first released in North America on 8 November 2005. It brings the SOCOM approach to PSP through a third-person campaign and wireless multiplayer. The player enters missions with military equipment and the need to recognise threats before committing to an approach. Moving onto a handheld also required changes to the familiar console controls. The result places the series' interest in armed teamwork within a machine whose single analogue nub cannot reproduce the controller layout of the PlayStation 2 games directly.

cards.heading: Lock-on aiming adapts the encounter to one analogue control
cards.text: Holding the right shoulder button locks onto a target before firing, allowing the player to manage movement without a second analogue stick dedicated to aiming. Sniper rifles, assault rifles, machine guns and grenades provide different responses to the mission. The choice of equipment matters alongside identifying a target, since distance and the surrounding threats can make one approach more useful than another. Fireteam Bravo retains the need to read an encounter while adapting the physical act of aiming to PSP, making the hardware limitation part of the design rather than simply copying the larger console's controls.

cards.heading: Wireless play becomes part of the portable squad
cards.text: The game supports both local ad-hoc connections between PSP systems and infrastructure play through a wireless network. Up to sixteen players could compete online, with voice chat helping bring the series' communication-focused identity onto the handheld. Reviews were generally positive, and Fireteam Bravo became a portable branch of SOCOM with further sequels. Official online servers closed in 2012. Its original significance lies in the ambition of the package: a handheld tactical campaign accompanied by a substantial networked game, offered at a time when console-style online features were becoming increasingly important to portable systems.

main.title: The Matrix: Path of Neo
main.summary: The Matrix: Path of Neo is a 2005 action-adventure video game developed by Shiny Entertainment and published by Atari.

cards.heading: Playing Neo through the Matrix trilogy
cards.text: The Matrix: Path of Neo is a 2005 action-adventure video game developed by Shiny Entertainment and published by Atari. The game was written and co-directed by the Wachowskis, who wrote and directed the first three The Matrix films and the 2003 video game Enter the Matrix, also developed by Shiny Entertainment. Players control the character Neo, participating in scenes from the films.

cards.heading: Taking a different path through familiar scenes
cards.text: Players assume the role of Neo, with the objective of guiding the character through the events of The Matrix trilogy, supported by montages of edited cutscenes sourced from the films. Some levels imitate the scenes of the films, other extend them, or take entirely different directions. In some sequences, players can make choices to diverge from the events of the film; for instance, guiding Neo to escape an office building instead of surrendering to police, or choosing the blue pill instead of the red pill.

cards.heading: Combining combat and Focus
cards.text: Path of Neo combines close combat, weapons and a Focus ability. Attack and stun buttons link punches and kicks into combinations, while guns, hatchets, swords and explosives provide other ways to fight. Opening tutorials introduce melee, sword fighting and shooting; an action sequence adjusts the difficulty according to the player's performance. Filling the Focus meter gives access to stronger combinations. Further upgrades become available between missions.

cards.heading: Responding to Enter the Matrix
cards.text: After Enter the Matrix, Shiny examined what had worked and what its rushed production had left unresolved. Players' wish to control Neo became the centre of the next game. Rather than follow another set of characters alongside the films, the team could build encounters around his powers and perspective. David Perry and other developers recalled a less restricted project, with room to pursue ideas because they made an enjoyable action sequence. The change gave the sequel a clearer relationship between its chosen hero and what the player could do.

cards.heading: Motion capture and a revised engine
cards.text: Development of Path of Neo took place over a two-year development cycle involving a team of 60 to 80 staff, involving most of the team that created Enter the Matrix. Developers recounted that the pace of development was more relaxed than Enter the Matrix, with the final six months dedicated to testing and refining the game. Path of Neo was developed using an enhanced version of the engine from Enter The Matrix, featuring the Havok 2 Physics engine allowing for destructible environments, with a scene featuring 1,500 copies of Agent Smith showcased to demonstrate the capabilities of the engine. Rountree stated 4,000 animations were designed for the game's combat, mostly choreographed using motion capture and then manually edited to make moves feel "superhuman" and "fun to play", using techniques such as real-time inverse kinematics to create the illusion of realistic blocks.

cards.heading: The Wachowskis write a new ending
cards.text: The Wachowskis contributed as writers and creative directors, adding story material, re-editing film scenes and responding to the game's development. Laurence Fishburne recorded new Morpheus dialogue. For the ending, the team wanted a boss battle rather than simply repeat The Matrix Revolutions. The Wachowskis proposed a giant figure assembled from Agent Smith copies, preceded by their own pixelated avatars explaining the departure. The sequence treats adaptation as a chance to change the climax for play, ending the journey with a deliberately playful break in the fourth wall.

cards.heading: Revealing the game in 2005
cards.text: Atari announced Path of Neo in February 2005, and showcased it at E3 in May 2005 and the Tokyo Games Show in September. Preview coverage of the game was mixed: IGN described it as one of the best games previewed at E3 for 'Technological Excellence', finding its effects "incredibly convincing" and its engine featuring "impressive real-time performance" and "some of the best depth of field effects we've seen in this generation". GameSpot considered its action sequences were "extremely fun", but felt the visuals of the PC version were dated and inconsistent in quality. PlayStation 2 Magazine staff were "split" on the preview, writing the game "looks sensational" and featured "cooler characters, scenes and moves", although experienced camera and performance issues, and felt the game was "two years too late".

main.title: Guitar Hero
main.summary: Guitar Hero is a 2005 rhythm game developed by Harmonix and published by RedOctane for the PlayStation 2.

cards.heading: Harmonix and RedOctane make a rock game
cards.text: Guitar Hero is a 2005 rhythm game developed by Harmonix and published by RedOctane for the PlayStation 2. It is the first installment in the Guitar Hero series. Guitar Hero was released in November 2005 in North America, April 2006 in Europe and June 2006 in Australia. The game's development was a result of collaboration between RedOctane and Harmonix to bring a Guitar Freaks-like game to United States.

cards.heading: Following the notes on a plastic guitar
cards.text: The game features a guitar-shaped controller (resembling a miniature Gibson SG) that the player uses to simulate playing rock music. The gameplay is similar to GuitarFreaks, in that the player presses buttons on the guitar controller in time with musical notes that scroll on the game screen. The game features covers of 30 popular rock songs spanning five decades of rock, from the 1960s up through 2005, in addition to bonus tracks. Guitar Hero became a surprise hit, earning critical acclaim and winning many awards from major video game publications, and is considered one of the most influential games of its decade. The game's success launched the Guitar Hero franchise, which has earned more than $2 billion in sales, spawning several sequels, expansions, and other game-related products.

main.title: Pursuit Force
main.subtitle: The chase continues across the roofs of moving cars
main.summary: Pursuit Force is Bigbig Studios' PSP action game, first released in Australia on 10 November 2005. An elite police officer confronts the gangs of Capital State through missions that mix driving, shooting and spectacular vehicle changes. The defining action is a leap from one speeding vehicle to another, allowing the officer to fight its occupants and take control. A car is therefore a temporary position within the chase rather than the object that must always survive it. The next useful vehicle may be the one currently trying to escape.

cards.heading: The chase continues across the roofs of moving cars
cards.text: Pursuit Force is Bigbig Studios' PSP action game, first released in Australia on 10 November 2005. An elite police officer confronts the gangs of Capital State through missions that mix driving, shooting and spectacular vehicle changes. The defining action is a leap from one speeding vehicle to another, allowing the officer to fight its occupants and take control. A car is therefore a temporary position within the chase rather than the object that must always survive it. The next useful vehicle may be the one currently trying to escape.

cards.heading: Get close enough to make the jump
cards.text: Driving positions the officer for an attack, while shooting clears the destination vehicle before it can be commandeered. That relationship makes the chase a sequence of changing platforms, with each successful leap renewing the options available. Thirty missions also include boats, on-foot encounters and helicopter gunfire. Performance ratings unlock additional content, and progress grants abilities that help with later confrontations. The player has to balance speed and survival with the need to approach a target closely enough to change the situation, turning proximity into an opportunity rather than merely a collision risk.

cards.heading: A portable action film with one clear stunt
cards.text: Richard Jacques composed the score for a campaign organised around five gangs, each offering six missions. Race and time-trial modes provide separate driving challenges after the story's more elaborate set pieces. Reviews were positive, and Bigbig followed the game with Pursuit Force: Extreme Justice in 2007. The original's strongest idea is immediately understandable in motion: the hero can leave the car while the chase continues. That single stunt gives the PSP game a recognisable identity and lets driving and third-person shooting operate as parts of the same continuous action sequence.

main.title: Need for Speed: Most Wanted
main.summary: Need for Speed: Most Wanted is a 2005 racing video game, and the ninth installment in the Need for Speed series following Underground 2.

cards.heading: A racer arrives in Rockport
cards.text: Need for Speed: Most Wanted is a 2005 racing video game, and the ninth installment in the Need for Speed series following Underground 2. Developed and published by Electronic Arts (EA), it was released in November 2005 for GameCube, PlayStation 2, Windows, Xbox, and Xbox 360 alongside two distinct versions for Nintendo DS and Game Boy Advance. Another version for PlayStation Portable titled Need for Speed: Most Wanted 5-1-0, was released at the same time and featured alternative gameplay.

cards.heading: Rivals, revenge and police pursuits
cards.text: Most Wanted follows a street racer competing against fifteen elite rivals in the fictional city of Rockport. The climb through that group is also a revenge story: Clarence "Razor" Callahan has taken the player's BMW M 3 GTR. Police pursuits add another kind of contest alongside races, with Sergeant Jonathan Cross leading the department's efforts against the drivers. The more elaborate chases became one of the game's defining additions to the series.

cards.heading: The Black Edition and a continuing story
cards.text: Upon its release, the game received acclaim from critics and became a commercial success, selling over 18 million copies worldwide, becoming the best selling game in the series. Its success led to a Collector's Edition, known as the Black Edition, which provided additional content. A PS2 Classics version was available for PlayStation 3 via the PlayStation Store in May 2012, until it was discontinued the following year. The game was succeeded by Need for Speed: Carbon in 2006, which continues Most Wanted's story. A reboot by the same name, developed by Criterion Games, was released in October 2012.

main.title: Super Mario Strikers
main.subtitle: Next Level Games · GameCube
main.summary: Super Mario Strikers is Next Level Games' GameCube football game, putting Mario characters into fast five-a-side matches surrounded by electric barriers. A captain, three sidekicks and a goalkeeper form each team. Passing, shooting and tackling establish the sport's familiar purpose, while items and exaggerated physical contact turn its routes into opportunities for interference. The ball stays in play inside the arena, keeping the contest moving. The player has to create an opening while expecting the other team to use something much less sporting than an ordinary defensive challenge.

cards.heading: Football with Mario’s sense of restraint
cards.text: Super Mario Strikers is Next Level Games' GameCube football game, putting Mario characters into fast five-a-side matches surrounded by electric barriers. A captain, three sidekicks and a goalkeeper form each team. Passing, shooting and tackling establish the sport's familiar purpose, while items and exaggerated physical contact turn its routes into opportunities for interference. The ball stays in play inside the arena, keeping the contest moving. The player has to create an opening while expecting the other team to use something much less sporting than an ordinary defensive challenge.

cards.heading: Make space for the captain’s shot
cards.text: Only the captain can perform a Super Strike, a charged attempt worth two goals when successfully timed and scored. Preparing it requires enough space to complete the action without interruption. Shells, bananas and other items can disable opponents, giving the attacking team a brief opportunity to move or shoot. Ordinary passes remain important because they can create a faster opening than a prolonged special move. The player continually weighs the reliable immediate attempt against the greater reward attached to a shot that leaves its striker exposed for longer.

cards.heading: A physical sport suited to a shared screen
cards.text: Next Level Games brought experience from NHL Hitz Pro to the game's forceful tackles and rapid changes of possession. Bowser can enter the arena to disrupt both sides, giving the match another temporary problem. Released first in Europe as Mario Smash Football in 2005, it became the beginning of a separate Mario sports series. The original's clarity comes from keeping the destination simple. The ball still has to cross the goal line, but almost everything between recovering possession and taking the shot can become a comic act of sabotage.

main.title: Amped 3
main.subtitle: A snowboarding trip takes a strange turn
main.summary: Amped 3 is Indie Built's Xbox 360 snowboarding game, released in North America on 22 November 2005. It follows a group of riders through a deliberately eccentric story while allowing the player to explore several mountain resorts. Challenges scattered across the slopes provide ways to earn money, respect and new equipment. The boarding remains the centre of the experience, but its presentation moves away from a restrained sporting tone. Hand puppets, animation and other visual styles turn the scenes between runs into unexpected changes of mood and medium.

cards.heading: A snowboarding trip takes a strange turn
cards.text: Amped 3 is Indie Built's Xbox 360 snowboarding game, released in North America on 22 November 2005. It follows a group of riders through a deliberately eccentric story while allowing the player to explore several mountain resorts. Challenges scattered across the slopes provide ways to earn money, respect and new equipment. The boarding remains the centre of the experience, but its presentation moves away from a restrained sporting tone. Hand puppets, animation and other visual styles turn the scenes between runs into unexpected changes of mood and medium.

cards.heading: A mountain offers several reasons to take another run
cards.text: Some challenges ask for particular tricks, while others involve racing, collecting objects or matching a professional rider. Sleds and snowmobiles provide further variations. Respect unlocks new mountain areas and advances the story, making optional-looking activities part of the route through the campaign. The player can choose a nearby challenge that suits the available terrain or return to improve an earlier performance. Progress therefore grows from repeated use of the resorts, as a familiar slope becomes a place to attempt a different trick, earn another reward or reach the next opening.

cards.heading: The series trades sporting restraint for visual invention
cards.text: The third and final Amped game was published by 2K after the earlier Xbox entries. Its unusual story follows a disputed holiday fund and a cast whose problems quickly become more extravagant than a conventional snowboarding competition. Two-player minigames offer local diversions, while online features focused on a high-score leaderboard rather than shared riding. Amped 3's character comes from the contrast between traversable mountain spaces and scenes that refuse to keep one visual style. It treats the snowboarding trip as the foundation for a much stranger comedy about the people taking it.

main.title: Project Gotham Racing 3
main.subtitle: Supercars become the face of a new console
main.summary: Project Gotham Racing 3 accompanied Xbox 360's North American launch on 22 November 2005. Bizarre Creations concentrated its city-racing series on high-performance cars, carrying the Kudos scoring system into a new generation of hardware. Winning races remained important, while the quality of a slide or a clean passage through a bend could build another measure of success. The road was both a route to the finish and a place to perform.

cards.heading: A new starting grid
cards.text: Project Gotham Racing 3 accompanied Xbox 360's North American launch on 22 November 2005. Bizarre Creations concentrated its city-racing series on high-performance cars, carrying the Kudos scoring system into a new generation of hardware. Winning races remained important, while the quality of a slide or a clean passage through a bend could build another measure of success. The road was both a route to the finish and a place to perform.

cards.heading: The corner is part of the score
cards.text: Kudos reward more than a fast lap. Powerslides, drafting and other manoeuvres offer opportunities to earn points, with a corner judged through its approach, turn and exit. A driver can arrive at the finish having made different choices from a rival with a similar time. The system encourages repeated attempts at the same streets: a bend that once interrupted the lap can become a reliable place to link speed with a controlled slide.

cards.heading: Inside the supercar
cards.text: The cockpit view places working instruments and carefully modelled interiors around the road. A supercar's body is still visible in the external cameras, but the interior supplies another connection with the vehicle: the dashboard occupies the foreground while buildings and barriers sweep past the windscreen. Cars from makers including Ferrari and Lamborghini give the collection recognisable shapes. Their differences in handling remain important even within a selection devoted to very fast machinery.

cards.heading: Racing becomes a broadcast
cards.text: Gotham TV gave the original online release a way to turn races into something other players could watch. Replays and live competition extended the game's presentation beyond a driver's own event, linking personal results to the wider Xbox Live community. Garages supplied a quieter counterpart, displaying the cars collected along the way. Together these features placed racing, watching and collecting inside a single view of an international motorsport scene.
